beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Optimizing GPU Usage on AICR. How to request the right GPU, measure what your job actually uses, and right-size it, so your work runs sooner and wastes nothing.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. A GPU job that finished is not a GPU job that used the GPU. Many jobs leave the card waiting most of the time. This lecture is a set of measuring instruments: how to confirm you have the GPU, how to watch it live, how to profile it, how to fix the usual bottleneck, how to read memory against utilization, when to add GPUs, and the loop that ties it all together. Measure first. Change second.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. GPU utilization: the share of the last second in which the GPU was running any work at all. VRAM: the GPU's own memory, where your model and your batch live. DataLoader: the part of PyTorch that reads and batches your data and hands it to the GPU. Profiler: a tool that says where the time went. BF16: a sixteen-bit number format that keeps the range of thirty-two-bit floats. And DDP: distributed data parallel, one model copy per GPU.

beats.act: I · Do You Have The GPU?
beats.narration_text: Start where the work can quietly go wrong. If the CUDA module isn't loaded, PyTorch runs on the CPU and raises no error at all. A typo in the GPU request lands you on the wrong kind of node. And a leftover CUDA visible devices setting from an earlier shell can hide the card you were given.

beats.narration_text: AICR has two GPU families and four GPU partitions. B200 devel and B200 batch, with one hundred ninety-two gigabytes of memory per card. RTX devel and RTX batch, with ninety-six. beats.act: I · Do You Have The GPU?
beats.narration_text: Never trust that you got what you asked for. The workshop's verify script runs in under five seconds and checks five things. Is CUDA reachable. How many GPUs, which model, how much memory. What CUDA visible devices says. Does NVIDIA S M I agree. And a tensor round trip: CPU to GPU and back. Is available only means PyTorch can see a GPU. The round trip proves it can use it.

beats.narration_text: About that variable. Slurm sets CUDA visible devices to tell your program which GPUs are yours. Zero means one GPU. Zero comma one means two. Not set means you're outside Slurm, in an interactive shell, which is normal. Never override it in your script unless you deliberately want a subset.

beats.narration_text: One AICR-specific rule. A background process watches GPU utilization, and a job that holds a GPU without running anything is cancelled. So don't request a GPU and then sit writing code. Run the verify script first, profile in the devel partition in short sessions, and keep the batch partitions for jobs that are already tuned.

beats.narration_text: The fastest profiler is already on every node. NVIDIA S M I prints a snapshot; watch it every second in a second terminal. Two numbers matter. GPU utilization: eighty-four percent here means the GPU was running kernels for eighty-four percent of the last second. Healthy. Below fifty, something is wrong. And memory: twenty-four gigabytes of one hundred ninety-two in use. Twelve percent. Enormous room for a bigger batch.

beats.narration_text: A quick quiz from the workshop. Utilization twelve percent, memory ninety-one percent. What's wrong? The model is loaded, the card is full, and it's barely computing. Nothing on the CPU side is feeding it. That is data starvation, the most common problem of all, and it gets its own act.

shot.visual_intent: Two gauges side by side: 'utilization' fills to 12% and stays low; 'memory' fills to 91%; a job box sits loaded on a GPU while an empty conveyor from a CPU block brings nothing; label 'starved'.

beats.narration_text: Hold these two numbers as two axes, because people confuse them. Across: utilization. Up: memory. Top left is a loaded model that isn't running: a data pipeline problem. Bottom left is a GPU doing nothing at all. Bottom right is good throughput with memory to spare. Top right is the target: a big model, working hard. Eighty to a hundred percent utilization, seventy to ninety percent memory.

beats.narration_text: For a richer live view, N V I top. A dashboard that updates continuously, per process: GPU use, memory trend, power and temperature. On a shared node it answers the question that matters: is it my Python process using the GPU, or someone's leftover.

beats.narration_text: NVIDIA S M I tells you that there's a problem. A profiler tells you where the time goes. There are layers. System level: NVIDIA S M I and N V I top. Is the GPU busy. Framework level: the PyTorch profiler. Which operator or layer eats the GPU time. Timeline: N-sight Systems. Every CPU thread, kernel and memory copy in order. And kernel level: N-sight Compute. Is one kernel memory-bound or compute-bound. Most problems show up on the first two rungs.

beats.narration_text: The habit that matters most on AICR: profile in devel, run production in batch. In a B200 devel session you run the verify script, run your code for fifty to a hundred steps, profile, fix the bottleneck, and profile again until utilization is above seventy percent. Only then does the job go to B200 batch, unattended, and you read jobstats when it finishes.

beats.narration_text: The PyTorch profiler needs no extra install. Open a profile that records CPU and CUDA activity, records the tensor shapes, and writes a trace you can open in TensorBoard.

props.title: profile_window.py — open the profiler
props.code:
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity

with profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA],
    record_shapes=True,
    on_trace_ready=torch.profiler.tensorboard_trace_handler('./prof')
) as prof:
props.sparkLine: CPU and CUDA, shapes, a trace.

beats.motion_claim: The real code from the workshop prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Then the pattern that matters: profile a short window, never the full run. Twenty steps is enough. Step the profiler each iteration, and print the table sorted by total CUDA time. The top row is where you look first.

show.event: the loop and the table print

props.title: profile_window.py — a short window
props.code:
for step, (x, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
        if step == 20:
            break          # short window: 10-20 steps is enough
        out  = model(x)
        loss = criterion(out, y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        prof.step()

print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by='cuda_time_total', row_limit=15))
props.sparkLine: Twenty steps, sorted by CUDA time.

beats.narration_text: Reading it, in order. Gaps between kernels on the timeline: the GPU is idle, the CPU is too slow. Large copy entries: data shuttling between CPU and GPU. CPU total far above CUDA total: the work isn't really on the GPU. And DataLoader functions at the top of the CPU table: the pipeline, again.

beats.narration_text: Now the number one bottleneck. Picture a high-speed factory: the B200. It finishes a batch in eight milliseconds. The supply truck, the CPU data loader, takes fifty milliseconds to bring the next one. The factory stops and waits. Nothing is wrong with the factory. The supply chain can't keep up. And a B200 eats batches far faster than the cards you may be used to, so a loader that barely kept up elsewhere will starve it here.

beats.narration_text: The diagnostic is two timings. First, time fifty batches through the loader alone, with no GPU work at all.

props.title: starvation_check.py — the loader

beats.motion_claim: The real code from the workshop prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Then time fifty forward-and-backward passes on synthetic data, bypassing the loader entirely. If the loader time is larger than the compute time, you are data bound, and no model optimization will help until that's fixed.

props.title: starvation_check.py — the compute
props.code:
# Time just the compute (synthetic data, bypass the loader)
dummy_x = torch.randn(256, 3, 224, 224, device='cuda')
torch.cuda.synchronize()
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(50):
    out = model(dummy_x)
    out.sum().backward()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
compute_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 50 * 1000

# If loader_ms > compute_ms, you are DATA BOUND.

beats.motion_claim: The real code from the workshop prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: The fix usually lives in four DataLoader settings. Workers: CPU processes loading in parallel. Pin memory: page-locked RAM for fast transfer. Persistent workers: don't respawn them every epoch. And prefetch factor: how many batches each worker loads ahead.

props.title: loader.py
props.code:
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=256,
    num_workers=7,             # cpus-per-task minus 1
    pin_memory=True,           # always True on GPU training
    persistent_workers=True,   # keep workers alive between epochs
    prefetch_factor=2,         # batches each worker pre-loads
)

beats.motion_claim: The real code from the workshop prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Typical starting values. Workers: CPUs per task minus one, never zero. Pin memory: always true on a GPU node. Persistent workers: true whenever workers are above zero. Prefetch: start at two. The single biggest win in the whole workshop is one line: num workers from zero, the PyTorch default, to four or more. That alone often takes a job from twenty percent utilization to sixty or eighty.

beats.narration_text: Two percentages on the same screen that mean different things. Utilization: the share of the last second the GPU was running. Low means idle, from data or synchronization. A hundred percent sustained is fine. Memory: the share of VRAM allocated. Low means you could hold a bigger batch. High is only bad near the edge, where the job runs out of memory and crashes.

shot.visual_intent: Two independent gauges with their own needles: 'utilization' sweeps to 100% and gets a check; 'memory' climbs to the top edge where a terracotta 'OOM' mark sits; the needles move independently to show they are not linked. Act title top-left.

beats.narration_text: So read them as a pair. Low and low: the GPU is doing nothing; verify CUDA, check the data. Low utilization, high memory: loaded but not running; fix the pipeline. High utilization, low memory: healthy, with VRAM unused; increase the batch size. High and high: you're in good shape. And an out-of-memory crash: mixed precision first.

beats.narration_text: Batch size moves both axes. Doubling it roughly doubles throughput, as long as the GPU isn't already saturated and the memory is there. On a B200 with one hundred ninety-two gigabytes, memory sitting at fifteen or twenty percent means room for four to eight times the batch. Find the ceiling by binary search: try a size, see if it fits, halve the gap, repeat. Then run production at seventy to eighty-five percent of that ceiling.

beats.narration_text: Mixed precision is the next lever. PyTorch defaults to thirty-two-bit floats. Both AICR GPU families have tensor cores built for lower precision. The change is one wrapper: autocast to b float sixteen around the forward pass and the loss. Gradients stay in thirty-two bit on their own.

props.title: bf16.py
props.code:
from torch.amp import autocast

# Before (FP32)
out  = model(x)
loss = criterion(out, y)
loss.backward()

# After (BF16): add exactly this wrapper
with autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    out  = model(x)
    loss = criterion(out, y)
loss.backward()   # gradients stay in FP32

beats.motion_claim: The real code from the workshop prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Why BF16 and not FP16. A sixteen-bit number splits its bits between exponent, which is range, and mantissa, which is precision. FP32 has eight exponent bits and twenty-three of mantissa. BF16 keeps the same eight exponent bits and keeps only seven for precision, so gradients don't underflow and you need no loss scaler. FP16 bets the other way: ten bits of precision, but only five of exponent, which underflows. FP8 goes further still: four and three. Every step down trades numerical quality for speed and memory.

shot.visual_intent: Four horizontal bit-bars build, one per format, each split into a dark 'exponent' segment and a grey 'mantissa' segment with counts: FP32 8|23, BF16 8|7, FP16 5|10, FP8 4|3; BF16's exponent segment aligns exactly under FP32's and gets the terracotta mark; FP16's short exponent gets a small 'underflow' label.

beats.narration_text: What BF16 buys on this hardware. Activation memory roughly halves, so a much bigger batch fits. Matrix operations run two to four times faster on the tensor cores. And it is mixed precision, which is the safety net: the risky parts stay in thirty-two bit. Master weights, the loss, softmax, normalization. Autocast handles that for you. So the memory saving is partial, and the speedup is largest for matrix multiplies.

beats.narration_text: If memory is still too tight, gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory. Activations aren't stored in the forward pass; they're recomputed during backpropagation. Roughly sixty to seventy percent less activation memory for about thirty percent more compute. In Hugging Face it's one call. In custom modules, wrap the expensive layers. Use it when the batch is forced below eight, or when you're fine-tuning a very large model on one card.

beats.narration_text: Multi-GPU is the first thing people reach for when a job is slow, and it's often the wrong move. More GPUs amplify the efficiency you already have; they don't create it. The eighty percent rule: if a single GPU is already above eighty percent, you're compute bound, and adding cards divides the work. If it's below sixty, fix the bottleneck first, because four starved GPUs waste four times as much. And an I/O-bound job gets worse, since the cards now compete for the same files.

beats.narration_text: Here's what data-parallel training does. Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and takes a different mini-batch. After the backward pass they all-reduce: they average their gradients into one, and each applies the same update. Inside one node, over NVLink, that exchange is fast. Across nodes it's slower, so single-node multi-GPU is usually much faster per card than spreading out.

beats.narration_text: Before you ask for four GPUs, confirm your code is written for DDP. A plain script with gres equals gpu four gets four cards and uses one. Check that distributed is available and initialized, and that PyTorch sees as many devices as you requested.

print(dist.is_available())     # must be True
print(dist.is_initialized())   # True after init_process_group()

# Check: how many GPUs does PyTorch see?
import torch
print(torch.cuda.device_count())   # should match --gres=gpu:N

beats.narration_text: And measure the scaling. Throughput divided by the number of GPUs times the single-GPU baseline gives efficiency. Above eighty percent, the extra cards pay. Seventy to eighty is acceptable overhead. Below seventy, communication or I/O is the real bottleneck, and more GPUs won't help. Go back to the single card.

beats.narration_text: Every section was one bottleneck. In practice they come in that order of frequency, so here's the loop. Baseline: fifty steps, record throughput and utilization. Profile twenty steps. Diagnose: data, memory, compute, or communication. Fix one thing. Only one, or you can't tell what helped. Re-profile: did the bottleneck move? Record the gain. Repeat until utilization is above eighty, or the returns run out.

beats.narration_text: The decision guide, as a tree. Utilization under fifty? It's the data pipeline, and if workers is zero, that first. Fifty to eighty? Look at memory. Under forty percent: bigger batch. Forty to eighty-five: try BF16. Over ninety: smaller batch or checkpointing. Memory fine? Profile. Above eighty with healthy memory? Consider more GPUs only if the single card is truly saturated. And out of memory: BF16, then checkpointing, then a smaller batch. In that order.

beats.narration_text: After a batch job finishes, read its report card. Jobstats, from Princeton Research Computing, runs on AICR. Here is a real one, from a fifty-five-minute fine-tuning job on an RTX card. GPU utilization eighty percent: healthy. GPU memory seventeen percent: room for a bigger batch. CPU utilization thirteen percent: eight cores requested, barely one used. And a note: the job needed eleven percent of the eight hours it asked for. Request less time, and the queue moves faster for everyone. Make this a habit: under sixty percent GPU, fix it before the next run.

beats.narration_text: The pre-submission checklist, ideally run in a devel session first. The verify script passes. NVIDIA S M I shows over seventy percent during a fifty-step test. Workers is not zero. Pin memory is on. The batch uses at least sixty percent of VRAM. BF16 autocast is on. The script names the right partition. CPUs per task is at least four and matches workers plus one. The logs folder exists. And you've profiled twenty steps and read the CUDA column. Then cancel the devel session: four running jobs per user is the limit, and an idle one blocks you too.

beats.narration_text: None of this is PyTorch-only. Deep learning: every section applies, and in Hugging Face most fixes are one flag. Molecular dynamics: verify the GPU type before a long run, and multi-GPU scales well within a node. LLM inference: RTX cards for smaller models, B200s for the seventy-billion class. Custom CUDA or Triton kernels: everything applies, plus N-sight Compute for the kernel itself. And help is one email away: r c help at northeastern dot e d u.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Verify the GPU before anything else, because idle allocations on AICR get cancelled. Watch NVIDIA S M I: under fifty percent utilization means something is wrong. Profile twenty steps, and the top row by CUDA time is where to look. Low utilization with high memory is data starvation: fix the number of workers. High utilization with low memory: raise the batch size. Out of memory: BF16 first. Add GPUs only when one is already above eighty percent, measure the scaling, and read jobstats after every run.
